content: Arbidol is an antiviral medication developed by Masterlek, a pharmaceutical company based in Moscow, Russia. Chemically, the structure of Arbidol is based on an indole core, which is modified with various substituents at all positions except one. Arbidol is considered an alternative to Tamiflu, a well-known antiviral drug produced by Roche Pharmaceuticals, and is used in the treatment of avian influenza. The antiviral efficacy of Arbidol is still under investigation, with results ranging from strong acceptance within the pharmaceutical industry to skepticism in some quarters. Most of the clinical testing for Arbidol has been conducted in Russia and China. These studies have demonstrated its effectiveness against avian influenza, suggesting that it could serve as a more affordable and cost-effective option compared to Tamiflu. Preliminary evidence also indicates that Arbidol may be more effective in preventing infections caused by RNA viruses than those caused by DNA viruses. Additionally, it has been explored as a potential treatment for hepatitis C. The mechanism of action of Arbidol involves both immunomodulatory effects and specific antiviral activity against influenza A and influenza B viruses. It works by preventing the virus from attaching to and penetrating host cells. This is achieved by inhibiting the fusion of the viral lipid envelope with the host cell membrane. Furthermore, Arbidol has been shown to stimulate the production of interferons, enhance humoral immune responses, and improve the phagocytic activity of macrophages. Arbidol is available in the form of tablets and capsules, with each dosage unit containing either 50 mg or 100 mg of the active ingredient, Arbidol®. In terms of pharmacokinetics and safety, side effects in children primarily include hypersensitivity reactions to the drug. No cases of overdose have been reported to date, and allergic reactions are generally limited to individuals with pre-existing hypersensitivity to the medication.
